opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important questions in robotics right now. If you look at how we've trained most robot policies so far, it's largely through imitation: you collect demonstrations, often by teleoperation, and the model learns to copy what a human did. That gets you surprisingly far, but it puts a ceiling on things. You're bounded by the quality and quantity of the demonstrations, and the robot never really learns what happens when it goes off the path the human showed it.

When a robot learns from its own experience, a few things change. First, it sees its own mistakes. A demonstration is almost always a successful trajectory, so the model never learns how to recover when it slips a little or misses a grasp. If it's acting in the world, it ends up in those states naturally and can learn to get out of them. That's huge for robustness.

Second, you can actually exceed the demonstrator. With reinforcement learning, or any kind of self-improvement loop, the robot can discover faster or more reliable ways of doing a task than the person teleoperating it, who is working through a pretty awkward interface.

And third, it's about scale. Human teleoperation is expensive and doesn't grow as fast as you'd like. If you have a fleet of robots deployed and each one is generating useful data from what it's doing, and you can feed that back into training, you get a flywheel. That's what we saw work in language models with things like RL from feedback: pre-training gives you a strong prior, and then learning from the model's own outputs is what really sharpens it. I think robotics is at a similar point. We now have these generalist foundation models that are good enough to act reasonably in lots of situations, which means it's finally practical to let them practice and get better on their own.

r001.rationale: The response says robots acting in the world encounter their own mistakes and can learn what happens when they go off the demonstrated path and how to recover, linking their actions to task outcomes.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it matters for a pretty simple reason: the world is messier than any dataset we can collect ahead of time, and the robot is the one that actually has to live in it.

If you look at how we've made progress in language and vision, a huge part of it was scale of data. Robotics doesn't have that luxury in the same way. We don't have the internet of robot actions sitting around. We can collect demonstrations, and we should, teleoperation data is incredibly valuable for bootstrapping. But demonstrations have a ceiling. They show the robot what a human would do, through a human's interface, under the conditions the human happened to encounter that day. The moment the robot is in a slightly different kitchen, or the object is a bit heavier, or the gripper has worn down a little, it's off the distribution it was trained on, and it has no mechanism to recover.

Learning from its own experience closes that loop. The robot tries something, observes what actually happened, and updates. That's the thing that lets it go beyond the demonstrator rather than just imitating them. In our work we've seen cases where a policy starts from human data, is maybe fifty or sixty percent reliable, and then with a relatively modest amount of autonomous practice it climbs to near-perfect on that task. Not because we gave it more human examples, but because it found the small corrections that a human couldn't easily show it.

There's also a more practical argument. If you want to deploy thousands of robots, you can't have a human babysitting each one forever. Every failure in the field is, in principle, a training signal. If the system can't use it, you're throwing away the most relevant data you'll ever get: data from exactly the environment and exactly the embodiment that needs to improve.

And honestly, I think it's the only path to robots that get better over time instead of being frozen at whatever competence they shipped with. That's what we expect from people. You're not perfect on day one of a new job, but you get better because you do the job. I think robots should get the same deal.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot tries an action, observes what happened, and updates, connecting that feedback to learning corrections that improve its reliability on the task.

astra-6.text:
I think it matters because we can’t anticipate every situation a robot will encounter. You can program a behavior that works well in a particular setting, but then an object is a little different, or something moves, and the robot has to adapt.

Learning from its own experience gives it a way to make that adaptation: it takes an action, observes what happens, and uses that feedback to improve. That’s particularly important in robotics because acting changes the world. Watching someone pick up an object can be useful, but trying it yourself tells you whether your grip actually works.

The challenge is making that learning safe and efficient. We’d like robots to benefit from demonstrations and prior knowledge, while still being able to learn when they encounter something those examples didn’t cover.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot takes an action, observes what happens, and uses that feedback to improve; the grip example shows it learning whether its own action works toward the task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it matters because it’s very hard to anticipate everything a robot will encounter in the real world. You can program a particular behavior, but then the object is in a slightly different place, or it’s heavier than expected, or the surface is slippery. The robot needs some way to adapt.

Learning from its own experience gives it that feedback loop: it takes an action, observes what happens, and uses that to improve. And that’s particularly important for physical interaction. Seeing an object tells you something about it, but trying to pick it up tells you things you couldn’t necessarily infer just by looking. The challenge is making that learning efficient and safe enough to be useful outside the lab.

r001.rationale: The response says robots take actions, observe what happens, and use that feedback to improve, but it does not clearly connect those observations to whether the actions help achieve the robot’s goals.
